title: Perimeter and Area Grade 5: Formulas, L-Shapes and a Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master perimeter and area grade 5 with formulas for rectangles, squares and L-shaped figures, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable worksheet.
excerpt: Once a child can multiply, perimeter and area stop being about counting squares and start being about formulas. Here is how I teach rectangles, squares and tricky L-shaped figures in Grade 5, with a quick quiz to check the learning.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A Grade 5 student came to me stuck on a simple-looking problem: a rectangular garden 12 m long and 7 m wide, find the fencing needed and the grass needed. She had drawn every square inside the rectangle and started counting. That works in Grade 3. But by Grade 5, perimeter and area are meant to be a formula job, not a counting job — and the whole point is speed and accuracy on shapes too big to count. This guide covers exactly that: the formulas for rectangles and squares, how to crack compound L-shaped figures, and how to find a missing side when you are handed the area or perimeter instead.

You do not need special equipment. A ruler, squared paper for the first day or two, and a habit of always writing the unit. Let me walk through it the way I teach it.

The two ideas, kept separate

Half of all Grade 5 mistakes come from mixing up perimeter and area, so nail the difference before any formula. Perimeter is the distance around a shape — the length of fence, the ribbon around a gift. Area is the space inside — the paint, the grass, the tiles. Perimeter is measured in cm or m; area is measured in square units (cm², m²). I tell students: if the unit does not have a little square, it is not area.

Perimeter and area of a rectangle

For a rectangle with length l and breadth b:

  • Perimeter = 2 × (l + b). Add the length and breadth, then double it, because a rectangle has two of each side.
  • Area = l × b. Multiply length by breadth.

So for the 12 m by 7 m garden: perimeter = 2 × (12 + 7) = 2 × 19 = 38 m of fencing, and area = 12 × 7 = 84 m² of grass. Two formulas, no counting, done in ten seconds.

Squares are the easy case

A square has all four sides equal, so if the side is s, the perimeter is simply 4 × s and the area is s × s. A square of side 9 cm has perimeter 36 cm and area 81 cm². That is the whole story for squares.

Compound and L-shaped figures

This is where Grade 5 earns its marks, and where most children wobble. An L-shaped figure is just two rectangles stuck together. The method never changes:

  • For area: split the L into two rectangles with one straight cut, find each area, then add them.
  • For perimeter: ignore the split — walk around the outside and add up every outer side. The cut you drew is imaginary; it is not a real edge, so it is never part of the perimeter.

Take an L-shaped plot. The full outline gives sides of 10 m, 6 m, 4 m, 2 m, 6 m and 4 m as you walk around. The perimeter is just their sum: 10 + 6 + 4 + 2 + 6 + 4 = 32 m. For the area, cut it into a 10 m × 2 m rectangle (20 m²) and a 4 m × 4 m rectangle (16 m²), giving 20 + 16 = 36 m². Notice the imaginary cut appears in the area working but never in the perimeter — that is the single most common slip I see.

The counter-intuitive bit

Students assume a bigger perimeter means a bigger area. It does not. A long thin 20 cm × 1 cm rectangle has a perimeter of 42 cm but an area of only 20 cm², while a tidy 6 cm × 5 cm rectangle has a smaller perimeter of 22 cm yet a bigger area of 30 cm². Perimeter and area are independent. Getting a child to notice this once saves a dozen careless answers later.

Finding a missing side

The step up from ‘find the answer’ is ‘work backwards’. If you know the area and one side, divide to get the other. If a rectangle has area 48 cm² and length 8 cm, then breadth = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. If you know the perimeter, halve it first to get (l + b), then subtract the known side. A rectangle of perimeter 30 cm with length 9 cm gives l + b = 15, so breadth = 15 − 9 = 6 cm. Same two formulas, just rearranged.

Formulas at a glance

ShapePerimeterAreaExample
Rectangle (l, b)2 × (l + b)l × b12 × 7 → P 38, A 84
Square (s)4 × ss × ss 9 → P 36, A 81
L-shapeAdd all outer sidesSplit, then add areasP 32, A 36
Missing side (area known)—side = area ÷ known side48 ÷ 8 = 6

A practice routine that sticks

Fifteen focused minutes beats an hour of drift. What works for the parents I know: one day on rectangle and square formulas until they are automatic, one day splitting L-shapes, one day on missing-side problems, and a mixed day where the child has to decide whether a question wants perimeter or area. That deciding step is the real test — a child who can pick the right formula unprompted has actually understood it.

One honest caveat: do not let units slide. ‘84’ is not an answer; ‘84 m²’ is. In board and school exams, the missing unit is where easy marks quietly disappear, so make writing the unit a non-negotiable habit from day one.

Test what your child has learned

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly these skills — rectangle and square formulas, L-shaped figures, and finding a missing side. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 5 Perimeter and Area Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on rectangle and square formulas, L-shaped figures and missing sides. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 perimeter and area with formulas

questions.q: What is the area of a rectangle 9 cm long and 4 cm wide?
What is the perimeter of a rectangle 12 m long and 7 m wide?
A square has a side of 9 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area of a square = s × s = 9 × 9 = 81 cm².

questions.q: A square has a side of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: Perimeter of a square = 4 × s = 4 × 7 = 28 cm.

questions.q: An L-shape is split into a 10 m × 2 m rectangle and a 4 m × 4 m rectangle. What is its total area?
questions.explanation: Add the two areas: 10 × 2 = 20 and 4 × 4 = 16, so 20 + 16 = 36 m².

questions.q: When finding the perimeter of an L-shaped figure, the imaginary line you drew to split it is:
questions.explanation: The split line is not a real outer edge, so it is never part of the perimeter. You add only the outside sides.

questions.q: A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and a length of 8 cm. What is its breadth?
A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm and a length of 9 cm. What is its breadth?
questions.explanation: Half the perimeter gives l + b = 15, then breadth = 15 − 9 = 6 cm.

faq.q: What is the difference between perimeter and area in Grade 5?
faq.a: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, measured in cm or m, like the fence around a field. Area is the space inside, measured in square units such as cm² or m², like the grass covering that field. If the unit has no little square, it is perimeter, not area.

faq.q: How do you find the area of an L-shaped figure?
faq.a: Split the L into two rectangles with one straight cut, find the area of each with length × breadth, then add the two areas together. The cut line is only a guide — it never affects the perimeter.

faq.q: How do you find a missing side when the area is given?
faq.a: Divide the area by the side you know. For example, if the area is 48 cm² and the length is 8 cm, the breadth is 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm. If a perimeter is given instead, halve it first to get length + breadth, then subtract the known side.

faq.q: Does a bigger perimeter always mean a bigger area?
faq.a: No, and this trips up many students. A 20 cm × 1 cm rectangle has a large perimeter of 42 cm but a tiny area of 20 cm², while a 6 cm × 5 cm rectangle has a smaller perimeter of 22 cm and a bigger area of 30 cm². The two are independent.
